title: Community knowledge is frequently gathered without gaining policy power, creating capacity and evidence loops that weaken climate, nature, and social-justice delivery
source_unit: New Philanthropy Capital, Green Alliance, and ACEVO, Together for a fairer, greener future: Collective leadership in a time of crisis
geography: United Kingdom, with a focus on communities experiencing inequality, civil-society organizations, environmental and social-justice leaders, funders, policymakers, and access to nature

observations.period: 2025-2026; deliberative research on community power and cross-sector collaboration

denominator.unit: year-long Everyone's Environment Leaders deliberative programme involving senior civil-society leaders, grassroots activists, policy professionals, and people with lived experience

knowledge_to_influence_gap.value: community knowledge is often gathered, quoted, or consulted without consistently shaping policy, funding, governance, or delivery

power_problem.value: exclusion of lived experience is framed as a power problem, not only a representation problem

collaboration_route.value: lasting change requires infrastructure that connects community trust, knowledge, and legitimacy with institutional resources, access, and decision-making power

observations.method: Deliberative and qualitative work through the Everyone's Environment Leaders programme, workshops with grassroots activists, policy professionals, and people with lived experience, and cross-sector partner reflection; not a probability survey or impact evaluation.
observations.uncertainty: The report synthesizes participant experience and organizational analysis; it does not estimate prevalence, compare intervention effects, or establish that every policy system excludes community knowledge in the same way.
observations.subgroup: People experiencing inequality, grassroots and community organizations, environmental and social-justice groups, funders, policymakers, and civil-society leaders.
observations.counterinterpretation: Consultation can sometimes influence decisions even when formal co-governance is absent; technical evidence and administrative standards may protect accountability when combined with meaningful community input.

observations.period: 2025-2026; self-reinforcing barriers to community participation in policymaking

denominator.unit: reported reinforcing loops identified by the report

grassroots_capacity_loop.value: community organizations often lack time, funding, and administrative capacity to participate, leaving better-resourced organizations more visible to policymakers

evidence_influence_loop.value: policy and funding systems favor technical, written, and quantitative evidence, downgrading lived experience to supporting testimony rather than problem definition

missed_capacities.value: policymaking can miss richer problem analysis, narratives connected to everyday life, and community trust and legitimacy

accountability_gap.value: communities may be asked for experiences or ideas without learning what changed as a result

observations.method: Report synthesis of participant workshops, leadership deliberation, and case reflection on environmental and social-justice policymaking.
observations.uncertainty: The loops are an interpretive framework rather than a quantified causal model; capacity, evidence, and accountability barriers may interact differently across places and policy domains.
observations.subgroup: Smaller grassroots organizations, communities with less institutional access, technical policy systems, funders, national and local authorities, and communities facing climate and nature inequities.
observations.counterinterpretation: Technical evidence preferences can reflect legitimate needs for comparability and public accountability; the remedy may be hybrid evidence standards rather than replacing quantitative analysis with lived experience.

observations.period: 2025-2026; unequal access to nature as a test of usable public benefit

denominator.unit: report case and community deliberation on access to nature

access_beyond_proximity.value: usable access to green and blue space depends on safety, accessibility, quality, belonging, and having a say in design and management, not only geographic proximity

technical_target_risk.value: policies focused on measurable proximity can meet technical targets while missing the barriers faced by communities most excluded from nature

place_power_route.value: community influence over design and management is part of whether environmental infrastructure becomes a lived benefit

observations.method: Community-informed case analysis within a wider deliberative report on access to nature and just environmental transition.
observations.uncertainty: The case is illustrative and does not estimate access gaps or identify a causal effect of participation on use, health, biodiversity, or trust outcomes.
observations.subgroup: Disadvantaged communities, people facing safety or accessibility barriers, local organizations, public-space managers, and policymakers responsible for green and blue infrastructure.
observations.counterinterpretation: Proximity measures can be an important first-stage equity indicator; quality, safety, belonging, and voice may be addressed through subsequent design and management rather than replacing spatial metrics.

observations.period: 2026; proposed pathways from community insight to shared governance

denominator.unit: report priorities for civil society organizations, funders, and policymakers

priority_set.value: two-way community-to-policy pathways; trusted local infrastructure; co-owned narrative and governance; funded relationships and participation; and community-powered devolution

implementation_test.value: community power becomes meaningful only if organizations have time, resources, access, feedback, and decision rights rather than invitations to provide testimony

trust_route.value: shared ownership and visible feedback are proposed as routes to rebuilding trust while linking environmental action to housing, health, transport, economic opportunity, and inequality reduction

observations.method: Normative recommendations grounded in the report's deliberative process, participant experience, and case analysis.
observations.uncertainty: The priorities are recommendations, not funded implementation plans or evidence that devolution, co-governance, or local infrastructure will produce durable environmental or social outcomes.
observations.subgroup: Civil-society organizations, grassroots groups, funders, local and national government, environmental actors, and communities exposed to unequal climate and nature impacts.
observations.counterinterpretation: Shared governance can create decision delays, unclear accountability, or capture by well-connected groups unless roles, representation, resources, and evaluation are explicit.

Official 39-page report PDF produced through the Everyone's Environment Leaders programme with Green Alliance and ACEVO.

boundary: This record adds a community-power route from lived experience, local legitimacy, and unequal environmental exposure through organizational capacity, evidence standards, policy influence, shared governance, usable access to nature, and trust. It is a UK deliberative and qualitative report, not a prevalence survey, comparative causal evaluation, community-representative sample, or proof that its proposed collaboration model improves outcomes.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official NPC report page and 39-page PDF reviewed for methodology, knowledge-to-power framing, grassroots-capacity and evidence-influence loops, access-to-nature case, accountability gap, and five proposed priorities.
